source.text: *ርእይዋ፡ ለምድር፡ ወልብዉ፡ *በእንተ፡ ምግባር፡ ዘይትገበር፡ በላዕሌሃ፡ እምቀዳሚ፡ እስከ፡ ተፍጻሜቱ፡ ከመ፡ ኢይትመየጥ፡ ኵሉ፡ ምግባሩ፡ ለአምላክ፡ እንዘ፡ ያስተርኢ።
source.note: Complete Charles II.2 from printed page 6, including the wrapped final verb before II.3. Both actual complete selected-edition images agree. The running body has two asterisks; apparatus superscripts 9–16 are excluded. The complete printed appearance clause is retained with an explicit semantic and syntactic uncertainty note, without editorial restoration. Charles’s printed ተፍጻሜቱ is retained rather than regularized to the bare dictionary lemma.

transcription_uncertainties.issue: Printed words legible; the implicit subject and attachment of the circumstantial appearance clause remain uncertain.
transcription_uncertainties.treatment: Render both words in a visible English crux without supplying a subject, contrast, agent or reconstructed clause.

translation.text: Look at the earth and consider the work done on it from the beginning to completion[a]: none of God’s work changes[b] [while appearing; subject and attachment uncertain][c].

footnotes.text: The printed completion word ends in ቱ, not the bare ት of the dictionary headword. The vowel is compatible with a singular suffix, “its completion”; the neutral “to completion” does not identify a possessor. No possessive is supplied for “the beginning.” The source retains both printed asterisks, before “look” and the phrase introducing the work.

The colon introduces the observation signaled by ከመ. The printed negative and “all” are rendered as “none,” a use described in Dillmann’s Grammar §197(d). The suffixes in “look at the earth” and “God’s work” are not duplicated in English: §172(c) describes a suffix anticipating a following noun introduced by ለ. Charles’s note 13 proposes that words were lost by similar endings. The body has no visible gap, and this rendering inserts no Greek wording or contrast.

The two printed words are እንዘ፡ ያስተርኢ። Dillmann’s Grammar §170.5 supports the circumstantial “while,” and his lexicon (column 298, stem IV.1) gives the imperfect with the sense of appearing. Neither the subject nor the link to the rest of the sentence is certain; the bracket marks that uncertainty, not a gap. Charles’s note 15 proposes another connective conditional on his loss hypothesis, and note 16 compares Greek “appears” but questions the underlying rendering. Flemming also prints a circumstantial connector and an appearance form. The edited Aramaic fragments offer a comparison for the appearance sense, not a basis to import a subject or restore the clause.
